title: Modular Arithmetic
tagline: Keep numbers small under a modulus — addition, multiplication, and division (inverses).

intuition.analogy: A 12-hour clock: 10 o'clock plus 5 hours is 3, not 15. Arithmetic 'wraps around' a fixed size. Modular arithmetic is clock math with any modulus, used to keep huge intermediate results from overflowing.
paragraphs: When counts explode (combinatorics, DP), problems ask for the answer modulo a prime like 1e9+7. The reason: addition and multiplication play nicely with mod — (a+b) mod m and (a·b) mod m can be taken at every step, keeping numbers bounded.
Subtraction needs care: (a−b) mod m can go negative, so add m back: ((a−b) % m + m) % m. Division is the subtle one — you can't just divide; you multiply by the modular inverse.

Under a prime modulus, the inverse of a is a^(m−2) (Fermat's little theorem) or comes from the extended Euclidean algorithm. With inverses you can compute binomial coefficients and probabilities mod p.
intuition.keyIdea: Reduce at every step for +,−,×; for division, multiply by the modular inverse (Fermat or extended gcd).

steps.title: Add / multiply mod
steps.detail: (a + b) % m and (a * b) % m. Use 64-bit (or __int128) so the product fits before reducing.

steps.title: Safe subtraction
steps.detail: ((a − b) % m + m) % m keeps the result in [0, m).

steps.title: Division via inverse
steps.detail: a / b mod m = a · b⁻¹ mod m, where b⁻¹ = b^(m−2) mod m for prime m.

codes.title: modmath.cpp
modmath.py
codes.source:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def add(a, b): return (a + b) % MOD
def sub(a, b): return (a - b) % MOD
def mul(a, b): return a * b % MOD

def power(a, n):
    r = 1; a %= MOD
    while n:
        if n & 1: r = r * a % MOD
        a = a * a % MOD
        n >>= 1
    return r

def inv(a): return power(a, MOD - 2)    # Fermat's little theorem, prime MOD

complexity.time: O(1) for +,−,×; O(log m) for inverse
complexity.timeReason: Basic ops are constant; the inverse uses fast exponentiation.

pitfalls: Multiplying two ints near 1e9 overflows 32-bit — cast to 64-bit first.
Negative results after subtraction must be normalised by adding m.
Fermat-inverse requires a prime modulus and a not divisible by m.

dryRun.clickMoment: Division became multiplication by 4 — because 3·4 ≡ 1 (mod 11), 4 is '1/3' in this world. The verification 6·3 ≡ 7 confirms the inverse really undoes the multiply.
